meta.titre: Bouncer — one notch, one app at a time
meta.description: Bouncer decides which notch app you see on your MacBook. They all stay open, only one shows, and you switch with a two-finger swipe.

chrome.piedLigne: Bouncer, a utility for macOS 14 and later.

apercu.invite: Swipe across the notch, or click. In the notch:
apercu.debranche: Without Bouncer: both apps drawing in the same place.

heros.chapo: Your notch apps all stay open. Bouncer decides which one you see, and you change your mind with a two-finger swipe.
heros.voirCompatibles: See how your apps are handled

probleme.para1: Vibe Island, boringNotch, Alcove, Notchy: each one draws its own pill under your MacBook’s notch. Open two and they land on the same rectangle, one over the other. That’s the state you just saw when you switched Bouncer off.
probleme.para2: There is no coordination API, and no such thing as an “active notch app”. <fort>The only way out macOS gives you is to quit one app to use the other</fort>, then launch it again when you need it back. Bouncer handles that for you, and fast.

commandes.chapo: Take whichever is closest to hand. They all do the same thing: move one step through the cycle.
commandes.swipeCorps: Pointer in the notch area, horizontal two-finger swipe on the trackpad. No direction to remember: left or right, the gesture moves one step.
commandes.flechesCorps: Bring the mouse near the camera housing and two arrows light up on either side. When you’re not hovering, Bouncer covers nothing.
commandes.raccourciCorps: From any app, full screen included. Without a trackpad it’s the one command that makes you neither aim at the notch nor open a menu. It can be changed or turned off in the settings.
commandes.menuCorps: Bouncer has no Dock icon and no window to manage. Its menu lists the apps it found and shows at a glance which one holds the notch.
commandes.menuAttente: waiting, one click brings it back

moteur.chapo: Two routes, picked automatically from what each app’s binary accepts. There is nothing for you to set.
moteur.libelle1: to take an app out of the notch
moteur.note1: Fast route, measured end to end: 31 ms of propagation inside the WindowServer, 46 ms by the clock.
moteur.note2: Nothing to relaunch, nothing to reload. The app comes back where you left it.
moteur.note3: Some apps pin their windows in a private Space and ignore the hide command. Bouncer restarts them instead of giving up.
moteur.garantieCorps: Bouncer only touches the app in place once the new window has been <fort>counted on screen</fort> — not inferred from an API return code. If the target won’t start, or takes more than five seconds, the current app stays exactly where it is. You never end up with an empty notch, or with two processes killed.
moteur.refusCorps: No private APIs, no WindowServer injection: those are the tricks that break on every minor macOS update. An app that refuses to quit is never force-killed — it may well have something to save. Bouncer notes it and leaves the app alone.

compatibilite.titre: Does it work with your apps?
compatibilite.chapo: Four apps managed today, measured one by one on a real machine. Three more are waiting on a detection fix that has already been pinned down.
compatibilite.banc: Campaign of 5 September 2026, on an M4 MacBook Pro running macOS Sequoia. Every “measured” row comes from recounting the windows on screen, before and after hiding.

vibeIsland.note: Hidden and brought back in 46 ms end to end. A 740 pt band, seen by the scan.

cyclop.note: 49 ms end to end. A 700 pt band.

ghNotch.note: 47 ms end to end. A 414 pt band.

boringNotch.note: It creates its own Space and ignores hiding. Bouncer relaunches it: about a second.

superIsland.note: No private-Space API anywhere in its repository. Its notch surface never appeared during the campaign.

atoll.note: No private-Space API anywhere in its repository. Its notch surface never appeared during the campaign.

dynamicNotch.note: Its SkyLightOperator hands the notch window to a private Space: relaunching is the only route.

notchNook.note: Hiding works, measured at 57 ms. Its window spans the full width of the screen, and the detection filter stops at 80%.

notchy.note: Full-width window, same cause. Once seen, it would switch by relaunch.

mewNotch.note: Full-width window, same cause. Once seen, it would switch by relaunch.

compatibilite.para1: Bouncer has two questions to settle, and they are independent: can it see the window, and can it turn the window off. For the second, the dividing line is readable in the binary. An app that leaves its windows in your Space answers to hiding, and the switch is imperceptible. An app that pins them in a private Space of its own making steps outside that: Bouncer takes the other route and restarts it.
compatibilite.para2: For the first, the detection filter stops at 80% of the screen width, so a notch app is never confused with the Dock or a system overlay. Three apps draw across the full width and slip through it. <fort>The cause is measured to the point</fort>, and the fix needs a second criterion, not just a higher threshold.
compatibilite.para3: The test runs once, when the app is first found: Bouncer remembers the route that worked and doesn’t start over on every switch. The full campaign, machine and method included, is in the <lien>compatibility matrix</lien>.
compatibilite.verifierCorps: Once Bouncer is installed, this command lists the apps it found under your notch, with the verdict it gave each one.

prerequis.chapo: Four things, and you probably already have three of them.
prerequis.item1Corps: The lifecycle APIs and the interface are written for those versions.
prerequis.item2Corps: 14- and 16-inch Apple Silicon MacBook Pro, 13- and 15-inch M2, M3, M4 MacBook Air. With an external display as your main one, Bouncer finds the built-in screen that carries the notch by itself.
prerequis.item3Corps: One permission, asked for on first launch. It’s what lets Bouncer read the window list and hide other apps’ windows. Without it, Bouncer touches nothing.
prerequis.item4Corps: Bouncer is a stage manager, not a notch widget. With no third-party app installed it has nothing to arbitrate, and it tells you so right in the welcome guide.

installation.chapo: One line in the terminal, or an archive to drag across.
installation.sousLaCommande: Bouncer installs into Applications and opens normally.
installation.archive1: Download the .zip archive from the releases page.
installation.archive3: Drag Bouncer into your Applications folder.
installation.citationGatekeeper: “macOS cannot verify that Bouncer is free of malware.”
installation.expliqueGatekeeper: That’s what you’ll see on first launch, and it’s normal. macOS doesn’t know who wrote Bouncer: Apple charges developers €99 a year for an identity it recognises on sight, and Bouncer doesn’t pay it. The block is about that missing identity, not about the contents of the app: it is neither damaged nor infected.
installation.gatekeeper1: Double-click Bouncer and let macOS refuse.
installation.gatekeeper2: Open System Settings, then Privacy & Security.
installation.gatekeeper3: Scroll down to the message about Bouncer and click “Open Anyway”.
installation.apres1: Later launches go straight through. Through Homebrew you never see that screen, because the cask strips the quarantine attribute itself. That’s a Gatekeeper workaround we write ourselves, and it goes away the day Bouncer is notarised by Apple.
installation.apres2: On first launch, a welcome guide shows you where Bouncer sits in the menu bar, checks the Accessibility permission live, and has you try the gesture.

faq.q1: Do my apps close when I switch?
faq.r1: Not on the fast route: the app is hidden, stays in memory and comes back in the state you left it. On the relaunch route, yes, it restarts. The table says row by row what to expect.
faq.r2: Nothing. Bouncer is free and the code is public on GitHub. There’s no account, no licence key, no trial.
faq.r3: Whichever you like. The gesture doesn’t pick a direction, it moves one step through the cycle, and the cycle loops. There’s nothing to memorise.
faq.q4: What if the app doesn’t restart?
faq.r4: The app in place doesn’t move. Bouncer turns on before it turns off: until the new window is counted on screen, it touches nothing. After five seconds it gives up and leaves the notch as it was.
faq.q5: Does it run in the background all the time?
faq.r5: Yes, with no window and no Dock icon. Bouncer re-checks the windows every two seconds by default, and that interval is adjustable from one to thirty seconds.
faq.q6: How do I get rid of it?
faq.r6: Drag Bouncer to the Trash, or brew uninstall --cask donpaco13/tap/bouncer. Nothing is left running: your notch apps go back to what they were before, overlap included.

fin.titre: One notch, one app at a time
fin.corps: Free, open source, one macOS permission to grant.
